newsitem.title: USA: Survey suggests U.S. health costs will surge again.
newsitem.headline: Survey suggests U.S. health costs will surge again.

text.p: U.S. health costs will soon start outstripping inflation once again, and rising prices will particularly affect small businesses and middle class families, a new study said on Wednesday.

The study for the nonpartisan National Coalition on Health Care found that health costs would rise at least twice as fast as inflation over the next five years. The past two years have seen relatively low cost increases and the rise of managed health care.
"The data confirms the trend we have anticipated, that health care cost pressures have resumed and will continue to build," coalition president Dr. Henry Simmons said.
"Unfortunately it appears that the 'easy' savings in health cost have already been squeezed out. What we're seeing now is a return to the inflationary pressures of the '80s," he said.
The study predicted that health costs would rise 6.4 percent this year, with middle class families earning from $20,000 to $60,000 paying about $500 to $1,000 more on health this year alone.
Over the next five years, married couples with children will pay 5.5 percent above inflation and single-parent families will pay as much as 10 percent above inflation for health care, it forecasts.

A typical family will spend $2,000 on health this year, with about half of that going to insurance premiums. Those bills will reflect a hidden subsidy to cover the cost of caring for the roughly 40 million Americans who are uninsured.
Although all businesses would feel the inflationary trend, smaller businesses had less clout in the insurance marketplace and faced premium increases of about 6.3 percent a year, it said.
The study estimated that national health care expenditure exceeded $1 trillion last year, and would grow to $1.5 trillion by 2002, or almost 15 percent of the gross domestic product.

The coalition is a nonpartisan organisation including business, labour and consumer groups. The Kaiser Family foundation helped finance the study, which was conducted by Kenneth Thorpe of Tulane University, a former Clinton administration health official.
